t: Under the double-entry system of book-keeping, every transaction affects:
o: Only one account, which is debited
Only the cash account and one other account
At least two accounts, with equal debit and credit
Two accounts, both of which are debited
e: Double entry records the dual aspect of each transaction: total debits always equal total credits, which is what makes the trial balance agree.

t: The accounting convention that requires anticipated losses to be provided for but anticipated profits to be ignored is:
o: Materiality
Conservatism (prudence)
Consistency
Full disclosure
e: Prudence requires that provisions be made for probable losses while unrealised gains are not recognised; consistency and materiality deal with uniform treatment and significance respectively.

t: Which of the following is a personal account under the traditional classification of accounts?
o: Discount received account
Building account
Outstanding salary account
Salary account
e: Outstanding salary is a representative personal account standing for the employees to whom salary is due; salary and discount are nominal and building is real.

t: Under the accrual concept, a general insurer that collects ₹12 lakh premium on 1 January 2026 for a one-year policy should, at 31 March 2026, recognise as income:
o: Nil, since the policy has not yet expired
₹9 lakh, being the premium for the unexpired period
₹3 lakh, being the premium relating to the three months of risk already run
₹12 lakh, since the full premium has been received in cash
e: Accrual and matching require revenue to be recognised in the period in which the risk is borne; the balance ₹9 lakh is carried forward as reserve for unexpired risk.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: A trial balance agrees even though the purchase of furniture for ₹40,000 has been debited to the purchases account. This is an example of:
o: Error of omission
Error of principle
Compensating error
Error of casting
e: Treating a capital expenditure as revenue expenditure violates an accounting principle; since both debit and credit are of the same amount, the trial balance still agrees.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: A machine was purchased on 1 April 2023 for ₹5,00,000 with an estimated residual value of ₹50,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Under the straight-line method, the written-down value on 31 March 2026 is:
e: Annual depreciation is (5,00,000 − 50,000)/5 = ₹90,000; after three years the accumulated depreciation is ₹2,70,000 and the WDV is ₹5,00,000 − ₹2,70,000 = ₹2,30,000.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: Which one of the following errors will NOT be disclosed by a trial balance?
o: Sale of ₹8,000 to Rao completely omitted from the books
Discount allowed of ₹600 posted twice to the discount account
₹5,000 received from Mehta posted to the credit of Mehta as ₹500
Purchases book overcast by ₹1,000
e: A complete omission leaves both debit and credit sides equally short, so the trial balance still agrees; the other errors affect only one side and create a difference.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: Under the written-down value method of depreciation, the amount of depreciation charged each year:
o: Is charged only in the year of purchase
Declines every year because it is computed on the reducing book value
Increases every year to reflect rising maintenance cost
Remains constant over the useful life of the asset
e: WDV applies a fixed percentage to the opening book value, which falls each year, so the charge is highest in the first year and reduces thereafter.

t: Under AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements), the purchase of fixed assets by a general insurer is classified as:
o: Cash flow from operating activities
A non-cash item excluded from the statement
Cash flow from financing activities
Cash flow from investing activities
e: Acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments are investing activities; operating flows relate to the principal revenue-producing activities and financing flows to equity and borrowings.

t: IRDAI requires general insurers to present the cash flow statement under which method?
o: Modified net-profit method
Indirect method
Either method at the insurer's option
Direct method
e: The IRDAI (Preparation of Financial Statements and Auditor's Report) Regulations require insurers to prepare the receipts and payments account (cash flow) under the direct method, unlike most companies which may choose.

t: A general insurer has gross written premium of ₹3,000 crore and net written premium of ₹2,100 crore. Its retention ratio is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Retention ratio = net written premium ÷ gross written premium = 2,100/3,000 = 70%; the balance 30% has been ceded to reinsurers.

t: AS 5 deals with:
o: Valuation of inventories
Accounting for fixed assets
Revenue recognition
Net profit or loss for the period, prior period items and changes in accounting policies
e: AS 5 prescribes classification and disclosure of extraordinary and prior period items and of changes in accounting policies; AS 2, AS 10 and AS 9 cover the other topics.

t: A company changes its method of depreciation from WDV to SLM. According to AS 5 read with AS 10, this change:
o: Is treated as a change in accounting estimate and applied prospectively, with disclosure of its effect
Is a prior period item and adjusted against opening reserves
Is not permitted once an asset has been put to use
Requires the restatement of all previously issued financial statements
e: Under the revised AS 10 (2016), a change in depreciation method is a change in estimate; the effect is given prospectively and the nature and amount must be disclosed.

t: As per Section 96 of the Companies Act 2013, every company (other than a one-person company) must hold its annual general meeting within:
o: Six months from the close of the financial year
Three months from the close of the financial year
Twelve months from the close of the financial year
Nine months from the close of the financial year
e: The AGM must be held within six months of the financial year end and the gap between two AGMs may not exceed fifteen months; nine months applies only to the first AGM.

t: Securities premium received on the issue of shares may be utilised by a company to:
o: Issue fully paid bonus shares to members
Pay dividend to equity shareholders
Meet routine administrative expenses
Repay a term loan taken from a bank
e: Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013 restricts securities premium to specified uses such as bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, premium on redemption and buy-back; it cannot fund dividend or operating expenses.

t: Under Section 139 of the Companies Act 2013, an audit firm may be appointed as auditor of a listed company for a maximum of:
o: Three terms of three consecutive years
An unlimited period subject to annual ratification
Two terms of five consecutive years
One term of five consecutive years
e: A firm may serve two terms of five years each (an individual auditor one term of five years), after which a cooling-off period of five years applies.

t: The pattern of shareholding of a general insurance company is disclosed in which schedule of the IRDAI-prescribed financial statements?
o: Schedule 5
Schedule 6
Schedule 12
Schedule 5A
e: Schedule 5 shows share capital, Schedule 5A gives the pattern of shareholding of promoters (Indian and foreign) and others, and Schedule 6 shows reserves and surplus.

t: Which of the following statements regarding the audit committee of a company under Section 177 of the Companies Act 2013 is correct?
o: It is required only for private companies
It must consist exclusively of executive directors
Its recommendations on auditor appointment are not binding and need not be considered by the Board
A majority of its members, including the chairperson, must be persons with ability to read and understand financial statements
e: Section 177 requires an audit committee of at least three directors with independent directors forming a majority and members able to read financial statements; the Board must record reasons if it does not accept its recommendation.

t: Under the historical cost concept, land bought in 2010 for ₹2 crore and now worth ₹9 crore is normally shown in the books at:
o: ₹9 crore
₹7 crore, the appreciation only
₹5.5 crore, the average of the two
₹2 crore
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Assets are recorded at acquisition cost and not written up for market appreciation unless a formal revaluation is adopted; this keeps the figures objective and verifiable.

t: Section 11 of the Insurance Act 1938 requires every insurer to prepare its balance sheet, profit and loss account and revenue account:
o: In the forms and manner specified by regulations made by IRDAI
In any format approved by its statutory auditor
In the formats prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India
In the forms set out in Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013 only
e: Section 11 delegates the form of financial statements to IRDAI regulations, which prescribe Forms B-RA, B-PL and B-BS for general insurers.

t: A general insurer is required to prepare separate revenue accounts for which classes of business?
o: Direct and reinsurance
Fire, marine and miscellaneous
Motor, health and others
Retail and corporate
e: Form B-RA must be prepared separately for fire, marine and miscellaneous insurance business, with segment-wise reporting of sub-classes within miscellaneous.

t: In the Revenue Account of a general insurer, 'Premium earned (net)' as per Schedule 1 is computed as:
o: Gross direct premium plus reinsurance accepted, less reinsurance ceded, adjusted for change in reserve for unexpired risk
Net written premium less claims paid
Gross direct premium less commission paid
Gross direct premium less outstanding premium
e: Schedule 1 starts with premium from direct business, adds premium on reinsurance accepted, deducts premium on reinsurance ceded and then adjusts for the change in unexpired risk reserve to arrive at earned premium.

t: Salvage realised on a settled motor claim is accounted for by a general insurer as:
o: Miscellaneous income in the profit and loss account
A reduction in the claims cost
An addition to premium earned
A capital receipt credited to reserves
e: Salvage and subrogation recoveries are netted against claims incurred in Schedule 2, since they reduce the net cost of the claim rather than generate separate income.

t: The operating profit or loss transferred from the fire, marine and miscellaneous revenue accounts is carried to:
o: A separate underwriting account not forming part of the financial statements
The Balance Sheet directly as a reserve
The Profit and Loss Account (Form B-PL) of the insurer
The Receipts and Payments Account
e: The P&L Account begins with the operating profit/loss from each revenue account, adds shareholders' investment income and other income, and deducts expenses not related to insurance business, taxes and appropriations.

t: Which of the following is correctly matched with its IRDAI schedule number in a general insurer's balance sheet?
o: Schedule 10 – Loans
Schedule 8 – Investments
Schedule 8 – Fixed assets
Schedule 13 – Provisions
e: Investments are in Schedule 8, loans in Schedule 9, fixed assets in Schedule 10, current liabilities in Schedule 13 and provisions in Schedule 14.

t: A general insurer wrote gross direct premium of ₹800 crore, accepted reinsurance of ₹50 crore and ceded reinsurance of ₹250 crore during the year. The reserve for unexpired risk increased from ₹280 crore to ₹310 crore. Premium earned (net) is:
o: ₹550 crore
₹600 crore
₹570 crore
₹630 crore
e: Net written premium = 800 + 50 − 250 = ₹600 crore; the increase in URR of ₹30 crore is deducted, giving premium earned of ₹570 crore.

t: As per the IRDAI (Preparation of Financial Statements) Regulations 2002, the minimum reserve for unexpired risk for marine hull business is:
o: 40% of gross premium of the year
50% of net premium of the year
75% of net premium of the year
100% of net premium of the year
e: The regulations prescribe URR of not less than 50% of net premium for fire, marine cargo and miscellaneous business and 100% for marine hull; IRDAI has since permitted the 1/365 method as an alternative.

t: Under Section 15 of the Insurance Act 1938, the audited accounts and statements must be furnished to IRDAI within:
o: Six months from the end of the period to which they relate
Three months from the end of the financial year
Twelve months from the end of the financial year
Thirty days from the end of the financial year
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 15 requires the audited returns to be submitted within six months of year-end, with IRDAI empowered to extend the period in specific cases.

t: 'IBNR' in the context of claims provisioning stands for:
o: Incurred But Not Reported
Intimated But Not Reserved
Insured But Not Registered
Incurred But Not Recoverable
e: IBNR is the provision for claims that have occurred before the balance sheet date but have not yet been reported to the insurer; it is estimated by the Appointed Actuary.

t: A premium deficiency reserve is required to be recognised when:
o: The gross premium written falls below the previous year's level
Premium is received after the commencement of risk
The expected claims cost, related expenses and maintenance costs exceed the reserve for unexpired risk of that segment
Reinsurance premium ceded exceeds reinsurance commission received
e: Premium deficiency arises when the unexpired risk reserve is insufficient to meet the expected cost of the unexpired portion of the contracts; it is computed segment-wise and certified by the Appointed Actuary.

t: Under a surplus treaty with a retention of ₹50 lakh and a 10-line treaty, an insurer accepts a fire risk with sum insured of ₹4 crore. The amount ceded to the treaty is:
o: ₹5 crore
₹3.5 crore
₹50 lakh
₹4 crore
e: Capacity of the treaty is 10 lines × ₹50 lakh = ₹5 crore above retention; the insurer retains ₹50 lakh and cedes the balance ₹3.5 crore, which is within capacity.

t: Which of the following is a non-proportional form of reinsurance?
o: Surplus treaty
Excess of loss treaty
Facultative-obligatory treaty
Quota share treaty
e: In non-proportional reinsurance the reinsurer pays only losses exceeding an agreed amount; quota share, surplus and fac-oblig share premiums and losses proportionately.

t: Reinsurance ceded by a reinsurer to another reinsurer is termed:
o: Retrocession
Fronting
Co-insurance
Pooling
e: Retrocession is reinsurance of reinsurance; fronting is issuing a policy to pass the risk almost entirely to another insurer, and co-insurance is direct sharing of a risk between insurers.

t: The control level of solvency prescribed by IRDAI for general insurers, below which regulatory action is triggered, is a solvency ratio of:
e: Insurers must maintain available solvency margin of at least 1.5 times the required solvency margin at all times; falling below 150% invites regulatory directions.

t: Under Section 6 of the Insurance Act 1938, the minimum paid-up equity capital required to carry on general insurance business in India is:
o: ₹200 crore
₹100 crore
₹500 crore
₹50 crore
e: A life or general insurer needs ₹100 crore of paid-up equity capital, whereas a reinsurer needs ₹200 crore.

t: Available Solvency Margin (ASM) of a general insurer is broadly:
o: The excess of the value of admissible assets over the value of liabilities, as determined under Section 64V
The sum of paid-up capital and gross written premium
The total of technical reserves held by the insurer
The market value of its investments in government securities
e: ASM is derived from Form KG as assets less liabilities after excluding inadmissible assets; it is compared with the Required Solvency Margin to arrive at the solvency ratio.

t: The minimum paid-up equity capital required to start a life or general insurance company in India is:
o: ₹50 crore
₹100 crore
₹200 crore
₹500 crore
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹100 crore for a direct insurer; ₹200 crore for a reinsurer (Section 6 of the Insurance Act).

t: A general insurer has an available solvency margin of ₹1,800 crore and a required solvency margin of ₹1,000 crore. Its solvency ratio is:
o: 1.80, which is below the control level
1.80, which is above the control level
0.56, which is below the control level
2.80, which is above the control level
e: Solvency ratio = ASM/RSM = 1,800/1,000 = 1.80 (180%), comfortably above the 150% control level.

t: Under the IRDAI (Investment) Regulations 2016, a general insurer must invest in Central Government securities not less than:
o: 20% of its investment assets
50% of its investment assets
10% of its investment assets
30% of its investment assets
e: The pattern requires at least 20% in Central Government securities and at least 30% in Central, State and other approved securities taken together (inclusive of the 20%).

t: For a general insurer, the combined minimum investment in housing and infrastructure under the IRDAI investment pattern is:
o: Not more than 10% of investment assets
Not less than 25% of investment assets
Not less than 5% of investment assets
Not less than 15% of investment assets
e: The 2016 regulations require general insurers to hold at least 15% in housing and infrastructure investments, with a maximum of 55% in approved investments (including other investments).

t: Section 27A of the Insurance Act 1938 prohibits an insurer from:
o: Investing in listed equity shares
Investing in Central Government securities
Investing policyholders' funds outside India
Holding deposits with scheduled banks
e: Section 27A read with Section 27 restricts investment of controlled funds to assets in India; the other three are permitted approved categories.

t: Unrealised gains or losses on listed equity shares held by a general insurer are:
o: Taken to the profit and loss account for the year
Credited or debited to the Fair Value Change Account and not available for distribution as dividend
Credited directly to share capital
Ignored until the shares are sold
e: Listed equity is valued at fair value and the difference from cost goes to the Fair Value Change Account in the balance sheet; only realised gains on sale pass through the revenue/P&L accounts.

t: Debt securities held by a general insurer, including government securities, are valued in the balance sheet at:
o: Market value as at the balance sheet date
Lower of cost and market value
Face value in all cases
Historical cost subject to amortisation of premium or discount over the remaining period to maturity
e: IRDAI requires debt securities to be carried at amortised cost; amortisation of premium/discount is recognised over the remaining maturity, and market value is disclosed by way of note.

t: An insurer's Investment Committee is required to meet at least:
o: Once every quarter
Once every year
Once every half-year
Once every month
e: The IRDAI investment regulations require the Investment Committee to meet at least once a quarter to review investment strategy, policy compliance and performance.

t: Profits and gains of a general insurance business are computed for income tax purposes:
o: Under the normal provisions applicable to any trading company
Under Section 44 of the Income-tax Act 1961 read with the First Schedule
Under Section 115JB only, as minimum alternate tax
On the basis of gross premium written during the year
e: Section 44 overrides the normal heads of income; profits are taken from the P&L account prepared under IRDAI regulations with the adjustments listed in the First Schedule.

t: Under Section 12 of the Insurance Act 1938, the accounts and balance sheet of an insurer must be audited annually by:
o: The Appointed Actuary of the insurer
An officer of IRDAI
An internal auditor appointed by the Board
An auditor qualified under the Companies Act 2013
e: Section 12 requires an annual audit by a qualified auditor; IRDAI additionally issues guidelines on eligibility and rotation of statutory auditors of insurers.

t: The control level of solvency ratio that every insurer must maintain is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Available solvency margin must be at least 150% of the required solvency margin; falling below triggers IRDAI action.

t: Combined ratio of a general insurer is calculated as:
o: Net incurred claims ratio plus net expense ratio (including commission)
Investment income divided by net premium
Gross premium divided by net worth
Claims paid divided by gross premium
e: Combined ratio = (net incurred claims ÷ net earned premium) + (operating expenses and net commission ÷ net written premium); a ratio above 100% indicates an underwriting loss.

t: A general insurer reports net earned premium of ₹2,000 crore, net incurred claims of ₹1,600 crore, net commission of ₹100 crore and operating expenses of ₹500 crore (net written premium also ₹2,000 crore). Its combined ratio is:
e: Loss ratio = 1,600/2,000 = 80%; expense ratio = (100 + 500)/2,000 = 30%; combined ratio = 110%, meaning an underwriting loss of ₹200 crore before investment income.

t: The 'current ratio' of an enterprise is a measure of:
o: Long-term solvency and capital structure
Profitability of operations
Short-term liquidity, i.e. the ability to meet current liabilities from current assets
Efficiency of asset utilisation
e: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; leverage ratios measure long-term solvency and margin ratios measure profitability.
